h2: Visual testing myths: what a code visual examination requires
html:
Visual testing myths: what a code visual examination requires

Visual testing is the method everyone thinks they already know, which is why its myths survive. The ones below cause rework, rejected reports and audit findings on structural, piping and tank jobs. The cross-method list is in conventional NDT myths.

Myth: AWS D1.1 visual inspection must be done by a CWI

D1.1 gives more than one route. Its inspector qualification clause accepts an AWS Certified Welding Inspector or Senior CWI under AWS QC1, an inspector certified by the Canadian Welding Bureau to CSA W178.2 at Level II or III, or a person the Engineer accepts on training and documented experience in structural steel fabrication, inspection and testing. Many contracts still require a CWI, so read the contract before staffing. NDT personnel doing UT, MT, PT or RT under D1.1 are a separate case: their certification is referenced to ASNT SNT-TC-1A or CP-189.

Myth: Inspect the weld as soon as it cools

Hydrogen-induced cracking can appear hours after welding, so an early inspection can pass a weld that cracks later. AWS D1.1 requires the final visual inspection of quenched-and-tempered steels such as ASTM A514, A517 and A709 Grade 100 to wait at least 48 hours after the weld is complete, and owner specifications set similar hold times for other high-strength or highly restrained welds. Visual inspection also starts before welding, with fit-up, joint preparation, preheat and interpass checks, because problems found then cost minutes rather than a repair.

Myth: Remote visual inspection is a lesser substitute for direct VT

ASME Section V Article 9 accepts remote examination, with borescopes, videoscopes, crawler cameras or drones, where the system resolves at least as well as direct viewing. The burden is to show it: the procedure is demonstrated on a fine line or resolution target at the working distance, angle and lighting, and every image is tied to a location on the component. Without that demonstration a video is a picture, not an examination. This matters most for remote visual inspection inside tanks and vessels, where nobody can check the result by eye later; see aboveground storage tank inspection.

Myth: Visual testers do not need NDT certification

Under SNT-TC-1A, VT is a method with its own recommended minimums: 8 hours of training for Level I and 16 more for Level II, with 70 and 140 hours of experience, plus general, specific and practical examinations. A "visual check" by an uncertified person is not a code examination, however experienced the person is. Visual testing training and the VT Level 2 course cover the theory online, and the VT simulator gives practice before the hands-on practical at the employer's facility.

Myth: Failing a color plate test ends a VT career

Not automatically. ASNT's published interpretations of SNT-TC-1A say a candidate who fails the Ishihara plates can still be certified if they can tell apart the colors or gray shades their method actually uses, as the employer determines. Near vision is a separate check: SNT-TC-1A asks for Jaeger J-2 at not less than 12 in., and the eye examination D1.1 asks of welding inspectors is repeated every three years. Keep each record current and on file; see NDT vision examination records.

Myth: A VT report is a pass or fail tick

A visual report that says only "acceptable" cannot be audited. It should identify each weld or area, the procedure and acceptance code, the light level and any aids used, measured values for profile, undercut and weld size taken with gauges, each indication with its location and disposition, and photographs where the procedure calls for them. For welds that need internal soundness, the report should also make clear that visual is not the final word: volumetric weld inspection follows where the code requires it. An ASNT NDT Level III can review report formats against your code before the next audit.
